Seats were later consumed via group-based licensing, now 21/25 per SKU (20 pilots + admin). Link the sanitized lab case study.

docs.title: SOP Health Monitoring
docs.text:
• ID: SOP-060
  • Title: SOP health checks and usage tracking
  • Owner: IT Administrator
  • Status: draft
  • Created: 2026-10-05
  • Review date: 2027-10-05
  • Applies to: All SOPs in this repo

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Procedures rot. Owners leave, systems change, and documents that nobody reads become fiction. This SOP defines how we measure whether each procedure is healthy: structurally sound, current, and actually used.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: Run scripts/sop-lint.py on every commit (CI does it automatically). It checks metadata, review dates, cross-references, and required sections. Separately, update last exercised whenever you follow a procedure — anything untouched for 180 days gets flagged as stale. Fix the findings or retire the SOP.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Covers automated validation (the linter) and usage tracking (exercise dates). Does not cover the quality of the procedure's content — that's what peer review is for.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Python 3 (stdlib only, no dependencies).
  • The linter at scripts/sop-lint.py.

docs.title: 1. Automated checks (CI)
docs.text:
Every push runs the linter via .github/workflows/sop-health.yml:

python3 scripts/sop-lint.py --strict

In strict mode, warnings fail the build. The check validates:

Check What it catches Required metadata Blank owner, missing review date, no title Status values Typos like actve, invalid lifecycle states Review dates Active SOPs past their review date Required sections Procedural SOPs missing TL;DR or tips Cross-references Links to SOP-XXX IDs that don't exist File references Backticked .md paths that don't resolve to a real file Retirement fields Retired SOPs without reason, replacement, or approver

Expected result: Green check or a specific list of findings. Findings get fixed in the same change window, not "later."

docs.title: 2. Usage tracking (human)
docs.text:
The linter can't tell you whether anyone actually follows the procedure. For that, each SOP carries an optional metadata field:

- **Last exercised:** 2026-10-05

Update it whenever the procedure is used for real — an onboarding, an incident, a quarterly review. The linter flags active SOPs untouched for 180+ days as stale. Stale means one of three things:

  1. Nobody needs it. Retire it (see workflows/sop-retirement.md).
  2. People need it but don't know it exists. Fix discoverability, link it from onboarding.
  3. People need it but aren't following it. That's a training or culture problem, not a documentation problem. Find out why.

Expected result: Every active SOP has a recent exercise date or a conscious explanation for why it doesn't.

docs.title: 3. Health review (quarterly)
docs.text:
Once a quarter, the owner reviews the full picture:

  1. Run the linter, confirm zero findings.
  2. List stale SOPs (180+ days without exercise). Decide: retire, promote, or investigate.
  3. Check the retirement log for patterns (are we retiring faster than we're writing?).
  4. Confirm every active SOP still has a named owner who still works here.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• CI is green on the latest commit.
  • No active SOP is past its review date.
  • Every stale SOP has a disposition (retired, promoted, or under investigation with a due date).

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Not applicable — this is a monitoring procedure.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: There are none. Every SOP is subject to health checks.

docs.title: Tips & pointers
docs.text:
• The linter catches structure, not sense. A SOP can pass every check and still be wrong. Pair automated checks with periodic human read-throughs.
  • last exercised only works if updating it is frictionless. Put it in the procedure's final step: "Update the Last exercised date." If it's a separate chore, nobody will do it.
  • Watch for the opposite problem too: an SOP exercised constantly but never updated. High usage with an old review date means the procedure is load-bearing and drifting from reality. That's the most dangerous kind of stale.
  • When CI goes red on a docs repo, fix it the same day. A broken health check that everyone ignores teaches the team that health checks don't matter.

docs.title: SOP Retirement
docs.text:
• ID: SOP-050
  • Title: Retiring a standard operating procedure
  • Owner: IT Administrator
  • Status: draft
  • Created: 2026-10-05
  • Review date: 2027-10-05
  • Applies to: All SOPs in this repo

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Defines how an SOP leaves active service. Retirement is a deliberate, recorded event — never a silent deletion. Past audits, control mappings, and incident reviews reference these documents; removing one destroys the evidence chain.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: To retire an SOP: record why it's going, what replaces it (or that nothing does), and who approved it. Mark the file status: retired, fill in the retirement fields, add it to the retirement log. Never delete the file.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Covers retirement of any SOP in this repository. Does not cover temporary suspension (use status: expired and fix it).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The decision to retire, with a reason in one of the categories below.
  • If the procedure is being replaced, the replacement SOP exists and is active.

docs.title: Retirement reasons
docs.text: Reason Meaning superseded A newer SOP covers this work. Point to the replacement. eliminated The task itself no longer exists (automated away, system decommissioned). merged Folded into another SOP. Point to the surviving document. obsolete The environment changed and the procedure no longer applies. No direct replacement.

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Update the SOP's metadata block:
  2. Status: → retired
  3. Add Retired date:
  4. Add Retirement reason: (one of the categories above)
  5. Add Replaced by: (SOP ID, or none)
  6. Add Retirement approved by: (name/role)
  7. Add a ## Retirement note section at the top of the document body explaining in plain language why it was retired and where to go instead.
  8. Add an entry to ownership/retirement-log.md.
  9. Check for references: search the repo for links to this SOP (control mappings, other procedures, the toil register). Update each to point at the replacement or note the retirement.
  10. Commit with the message Retire SOP-XXX: <reason>.

Expected result: The file still exists, is clearly marked retired, explains why, and every reference to it resolves.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• The SOP file is present and marked retired with all retirement fields filled.
  • The retirement log has a matching entry.
  • No active document links to the retired SOP without acknowledging the retirement.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Un-retire by reversing the metadata, removing the retirement note, updating the log, and re-entering the normal lifecycle at draft for re-review. Retirement is reversible; deletion is not — which is why we don't delete.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: There are none. Every retirement follows this procedure.

docs.title: Tips & pointers
docs.text:
• The most common retirement reason over time should be eliminated. If nothing is ever eliminated, the toil register isn't doing its job.
  • When a system is decommissioned, retire its SOPs in the same change window. Orphaned procedures for dead systems are how new hires get confused.
  • The retirement log is an audit asset. It proves the organization deliberately manages its procedures instead of letting them rot.
  • If you're tempted to just delete the file because "nobody uses it" — that's exactly the retirement that needs documenting. Future you won't remember why it's gone.

docs.title: Toil Identification
docs.text:
• ID: SOP-040
  • Title: Finding and measuring repetitive operational work
  • Owner: IT Administrator
  • Status: draft
  • Created: 2026-10-05
  • Review date: 2027-10-05
  • Applies to: All IT operational tasks

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: SOPs document how work gets done. This procedure identifies which of that work is repetitive enough to automate. The goal isn't documentation for its own sake — it's finding the tasks that eat hours every month so they can be measured, then reduced, then eliminated.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: List everything you do more than twice a month. Score it: frequency × time × error risk. High score + deterministic steps = automate now. Low automatability = document it well and keep it manual. And always ask whether the task should exist before you automate it.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Covers identification and scoring of repetitive tasks. Automation implementation is tracked separately per task.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Existing SOPs or runbooks for the processes being evaluated.
  • Rough sense of task frequency (tickets, calendar, memory — precision comes later).

docs.title: 1. Inventory the work
docs.text:
List every recurring task IT performs. Sources:

  • Ticket history (tag repeat issues).
  • Calendar (recurring maintenance, reviews, scans).
  • The SOPs in this repo (each one is a candidate).
  • Ask: "what did I do more than twice this month that followed the same steps?"

Log each in ownership/toil-register.md.

docs.title: 2. Score each task
docs.text:
Rate 1–5 on each axis:

Axis 1 5 Frequency Quarterly or less Daily Manual time Under 15 min Over 2 hours Error risk Mistake is trivial Mistake causes outage, breach, or audit finding Automatability Requires human judgment throughout Fully deterministic steps

Priority score = Frequency × Manual time × Error risk. Automatability gates whether it's worth attempting, not whether it matters.

docs.title: 3. Classify
docs.text:
• Automate now (score ≥ 48, automatability ≥ 4): Build it. Track in the register.
  • Automate next (score 20–47): Document well, automate when capacity allows.
  • Keep manual (automatability ≤ 2): Some work needs a human. Document it excellently instead.
  • Eliminate (low value, any score): Ask whether the task should exist at all before automating it. Automating a pointless task just produces pointless output faster.

docs.title: 4. Measure before automating
docs.text: For anything in "automate now": time it manually three times. Record the average. This is your baseline — without it, you can't prove the automation helped.

docs.title: 5. Review quarterly
docs.text: Re-score the register every quarter. Priorities shift as the environment changes. New hires, new systems, and new compliance requirements all create new toil.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: The toil register has a scored entry for every recurring task, each "automate now" item has a baseline measurement, and the quarterly review date is on the calendar.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: Not applicable — this is an assessment procedure.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: One-off incidents and novel troubleshooting are not toil. Don't try to automate what you haven't seen twice.

docs.title: Tips & pointers
docs.text:
• Time the manual task before you automate it. Without a baseline, "the script is faster" is a feeling, not a fact.
  • Start with the highest error-risk task, not the most frequent one. Automating a 5-minute daily task saves 20 hours a year; automating an error-prone quarterly task prevents the incident that costs a week.
  • The eliminate column is the most valuable one. Every task you delete is better than every task you automate.
  • Re-scoring feels like overhead until the first time a priority shift saves you from automating the wrong thing.

docs.title: Vulnerability Scanning
docs.text:
• ID: SOP-071
  • Title: Quarterly vulnerability scanning and remediation
  • Owner: IT Administrator
  • Status: draft
  • Created: 2026-10-05
  • Review date: 2027-10-05
  • Applies to: All in-scope systems (PCI, GLBA)
  • Compliance refs: PCI DSS 4.0 Req 11 (test security regularly)

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Find weaknesses on a schedule instead of discovering them during an incident. Quarterly scans satisfy the compliance requirement; the remediation process is what actually reduces risk.

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text: Run the ASV scan quarterly (and after any significant change). Triage findings: critical/high get tickets with 30-day remediation targets, medium/low go into the next cycle. Rescan to confirm the fix. Keep every report — auditors will ask for four quarters.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: Covers external/internal vulnerability scanning for PCI scope and general infrastructure. Does not cover penetration testing (separate engagement).

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• ASV vendor authorized for scanning (no surprise scans against third-party infrastructure).
  • Asset inventory current (you can't scan what you don't know about).

docs.title: Procedure
docs.text:
1. Schedule. Run scans quarterly, at least. Also run after significant changes (new firewall rules, new public-facing systems).
  2. Scan. Execute internal and external scans per the ASV scope. Save the raw reports.
  3. Triage (within 5 business days of scan completion):
  4. Critical/High: Create a ticket per finding or finding group. Remediation target: 30 days.
  5. Medium: Ticket, remediation target: 90 days or next maintenance window.
  6. Low/Informational: Track, remediate opportunistically.
  7. False positive: Document the justification, get a second pair of eyes, record the dispute.
  8. Remediate. Patch, reconfigure, or apply compensating controls. Update the ticket with what was done.
  9. Rescan. Confirm the finding is gone. A fix without a confirming rescan is an assumption.
  10. Archive. Store the scan report, triage decisions, and rescan evidence. Retain per the compliance retention requirement.

Expected result: Every finding has a ticket or a documented false-positive justification. Rescans confirm remediation. Four quarters of reports on file.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text:
• Rescan shows the finding resolved.
  • Audit trail: scan report → ticket → remediation evidence → rescan.

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text: If a patch breaks something: follow the change-management rollback plan, then re-triage the vulnerability with the new constraint.

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text: • Compensating controls: When a vulnerability can't be patched (legacy system, vendor delay), document the control, the risk acceptance, who approved it, and the review date. "Can't patch" without a compensating control is just an open vulnerability.

docs.title: Tips & pointers
docs.text:
• The triage meeting is the most important part. A scan nobody triages is just expensive noise.
  • Track mean-time-to-remediate for criticals. If it's drifting upward, that's a capacity problem masquerading as a security problem.
  • Keep a running list of recurring findings. The same vulnerability reappearing every quarter means the root cause (usually a broken image, a missed patch source, or a config that drifts) isn't fixed.
  • False positives deserve the same rigor as real findings. Sloppy disputes erode auditor trust in all your other judgments.
